planting.note: Plant container or bare-root own-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Le Vésuve is a pre-1825 antique China rose long grown own-root in old Deep South gardens alongside Old Blush and Archduke Charles.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Le Vésuve is an antique China rose dating to before 1825, bearing cupped, double blooms in soft pink that deepen and blush toward the petal edges as they age and as temperatures rise, much like its garden companions Old Blush and Louis Philippe. It flowers in repeated flushes from spring through fall and, grown own-root as China roses traditionally were in old Southern gardens, regrows true from the base after a hard winter or storm damage. It asks for little beyond decent drainage and full sun, tolerating summer heat and humidity with minimal disease and only occasional light pruning to keep its naturally rounded shape tidy.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root own-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Fortuniana is a vigorous once-blooming climber long used both as a Deep South and Florida garden rose in its own right and as the standard nematode-resistant rootstock for grafted roses in sandy Southern soils.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a fence, arbor, or other sturdy support to climb; Fortuniana is a vigorous, thornless-to-nearly-thornless rambling climber that produces a single spectacular flush of fragrant, fully double white flowers each spring, followed by handsome glossy foliage for the rest of the season. It is prized across Florida and the Gulf South both as a garden plant in its own right and as the region's standard rootstock for grafted roses, since its extensive, nematode-resistant root system lets grafted varieties thrive in the sandy, nematode-prone soils where own-root roses often struggle. Give it plenty of room to sprawl or climb, and prune immediately after its spring bloom rather than in winter, since flowers form on the previous year's growth.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Roses for Florida

common_name: Georgetown Tea Rose (Found Texas Tea Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root own-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Georgetown Tea is a Texas 'found rose,' rescued and named for the Central Texas town where it was rediscovered growing at an old homesite, similar in character to Duchesse de Brabant and Mrs. B.R. Cant.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Georgetown Tea is a Texas 'found rose' rescued by rose rustlers from an old homestead near Georgetown, Texas, and — like most tea roses that have survived generations of Southern neglect — it is exceptionally heat-tolerant and disease-resistant. It produces large, fragrant, loosely double blooms in soft pink to apricot tones that open from long, elegant buds, flowering nearly continuously from spring through fall in a warm climate. Grown own-root, it regrows true to type from the base after cold damage or hard pruning, and it needs little more than full sun, decent drainage, and an occasional light shaping to perform reliably for decades, much as it has at the old homesite where it was found.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Erlicheer is a fully double tazetta daffodil with a low chilling requirement, making it one of the few double-flowered narcissus that reliably rebloom and naturalize in mild Gulf South winters instead of blind out after a year or two.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Erlicheer is a fragrant, fully double tazetta daffodil bearing clusters of creamy white, ruffled blooms flecked with pale yellow, closer in form to a small gardenia than a typical trumpet daffodil. Most double daffodils need more winter chill than the Deep South provides and gradually decline into blind, non-flowering foliage after a season or two, but Erlicheer's tazetta parentage gives it the same low chilling requirement as Grand Primo and paperwhites, letting it rebloom and slowly naturalize where fancier doubles fail. Let the foliage die back naturally after bloom rather than cutting or braiding it, and leave clumps undisturbed to bulk up for a few years before dividing.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bulbs for Texas

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Grand Monarque is an antebellum-era heirloom tazetta long grown as a Southern pass-along bulb alongside Grand Primo and paperwhites, sharing their low chilling requirement and reliable naturalizing habit.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Grand Monarque is a classic antebellum Southern heirloom tazetta, bearing clusters of fragrant, creamy white flowers with a pale lemon-yellow cup on each strong stem, blooming in mid to late winter ahead of most other daffodils. Like Grand Primo, its low chilling requirement makes it one of the most reliable narcissus for perennializing in mild Gulf South winters, and it has been passed hand to hand between Southern gardeners for generations, often found still blooming each year at old homesites long after the house and garden around it have vanished. Leave the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and once established, let the clumps multiply undisturbed for years before dividing.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bulbs for Texas
